justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modestly bullish baseline trajectory anchored to recent price momentum and the broader market environment. At the one-day horizon, I assumed mean-reversion tendencies would keep the asset close to its last observed level, with the 132.1 estimate representing a slight upward drift consistent with short-term momentum. For the one-week estimate of 132.8, I incorporated a continuation of that mild upward trend while acknowledging that intraweek volatility tends to smooth out directional moves. The one-month estimate of 134.0 reflects a similar gentle drift assumption compounded over a longer period, consistent with historical average weekly returns in a range-bound to mildly bullish regime. None of these point estimates embed a strong directional call — they largely represent a base case of "more of the same."

The confidence interval widths widen substantially as the horizon extends, which reflects the standard square-root-of-time scaling of uncertainty. At one day, the 90% interval spans roughly 5 points, which is calibrated to typical daily realized volatility. By one week, that expands to nearly 12 points, and at one month to 24 points. These widths were informed by historical volatility levels, which I assumed to be moderate rather than elevated, along with some premium for event risk that tends to accumulate over longer windows.

Several sources of uncertainty shaped these intervals beyond simple volatility scaling. Macro policy signals — particularly interest rate expectations and central bank communications — can shift sentiment abruptly at any horizon. Liquidity conditions, earnings releases, and sector rotations introduce idiosyncratic jumps that are difficult to model in advance. I also factored in that month-long windows frequently capture at least one material news catalyst, which fattens the tails compared to a pure Gaussian assumption.

The primary risks that could push outcomes outside my stated intervals include an unexpected policy shock, such as a surprise rate decision or geopolitical escalation, which could easily push the price below 120 or above 150 over the one-month window. On the upside, a strong risk-on rally driven by better-than-expected economic data could accelerate the move beyond 146. On the downside, a broad de-risking event or liquidity crunch could drive sharp declines that exceed the lower bound. My intervals are intentionally wide at the monthly horizon to capture much of this, but fat-tail events by definition remain underrepresented in any fixed confidence interval.
